03:40 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 47s

Leave it alone. Recommendation with reasoning:

The cold-page window is narrower than it first looks. Walking the real arrival paths:

  1. Creating an auction goes through switchAuction, which ingests the probe response before the field even unlocks — state is never null there.
  2. Returning to an auction paints from the localStorage cache instantly — not null either.
  3. The only null window is first-ever visit by URL, and only until the first fetch lands (~0.5–2s). To hit it you have to read a page you've never seen, decide on a name, and commit it inside that window.

And the behavior in that window is now honest rather than broken: queueOp adds .stale before the if (state) gate, so the moment you commit the name the box grays and the gavel hammers — the app's standard busy signal — and the row lands with the add's own response. That's "stale means busy" working as designed, just for one extra round trip.

Against that, the fix would cost real complexity. Making state never-null via a synthetic empty snapshot poisons two latches: descModeSet would choose edit-mode from the synthetic blank and then hold a real arriving blurb in source view, and wasRevealed would latch false off the synthetic render, so a cold visitor who typed into an already-revealed auction gets a false confetti ceremony. Both are fixable, but each fix is a new flag or conditional — trading a ~1-second cosmetic delay on a rare path for two subtler state-machine hazards on paths the quals currently pin hard. That fails the Pareto test: it's not a dominating move, it's a trade, and a bad one.

So: ship what's here (it's all client-side — no Code.gs deploy needed, just your commit/push; the version span is already bumped to v2026.07.18-b). If the deferred paint ever bothers you in practice, the right follow-up is the full rethink — make the empty state a first-class representable state, with descModeSet re-keyed to the first unstale render and the fanfare latch made explicit — done as its own change with its own quals, not bolted onto this one.

Bug 5: code spans aren't literal

  • Replicata: Describe an auction with ecce `a*b*c` (any backticked text containing markdown syntax — snake_case identifiers with stars, regexes, shell globs are the natural victims).
  • Expectata: Backticks mean literal: a*b*c in code, verbatim.
  • Resultata: mdRender's inline passes compose wrongly — code spans get wrapped in <code> first, but the bold/italic/link regexes then run over the whole string *including the contents of the code tags just emitted*, so it rendered as code containing a live <em>. Safe HTML (the escape pass already ran), but wrong rendering.

Fix ([app.js:800-815](app.js#L800-L815)): code spans are stashed behind placeholders while the other transforms run, then restored. Two details I'll claim were worth the extra care:

  • The naive fix — split on code spans and transform only the text between — silently breaks [`y`](url) , a code span *labeling* a link, which works today. The stash approach preserves it, and the qual now pins that preservation explicitly.
  • The placeholder <<n>> is unforgeable by construction rather than by luck: the escape pass has already converted every author-typed < to &lt;, so no input can counterfeit one, and no emitted tag ever produces two < in a row. No sentinel characters, no reserved unicode, nothing an author could collide with.

Qual was written first and failed red on exactly the italics-inside-code symptom.

The fun piece: a fuzz battery for mdRender

New qual 2p4: 500 deterministic rounds of adversarial markdown soup — half-open syntax, nested markers, hostile HTML, javascript: links, and a forged <<0>> aimed at the new placeholder mechanism — asserting the renderer's promises under fire: never throws, pure function, only whitelisted tags materialize, attributes only on <a> (href http(s)-only), no placeholder leaks, no markup inside code spans. Seeded PRNG, so a failure is a *permanent* replicata: the assertion label prints the exact offending input.

Then I verified the battery itself, twice over, in a scratchpad harness:

  • Teeth: ran the identical soup against app.js with the pre-fix inline surgically restored — the battery catches it, auto-generating a monstrous minimal-ish replicata string.
  • Vacuity: tallying which tags actually materialized revealed that random soup had *never once assembled a valid link* — the entire <a> invariant set was passing vacuously (and <h3> never appeared either). Fixed by adding whole-link tokens (one of them code-labeled, so the trickiest composition is under fire too) — <a> now materializes 470 times per run — and the qual now enforces a coverage floor: every whitelisted tag must appear at least once, so the battery can pass vacuously exactly never, and deterministically can't flake.

is the right thing happening with timezones?
13:02 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m32s · 1m34s wall-clock time

Timezone audit — let me sweep every timestamp path in the system before answering.

Yes — the right thing is happening, and it's happening for a clean architectural reason: there is exactly one clock in this system. Every stamp — tini, tmod, tfin, tblurb, tbid — is minted server-side by new Date().toISOString(), always UTC, always the fixed 24-char YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ shape (and Apps Script's toISOString ignores the script's timezone setting, so the sheet's locale can't leak in). The three layers each do the correct thing:

Comparing — the two load-bearing comparisons are r[3] > tfin (is this bid row at-or-before the gavel) and the tblurb compare-and-swap. Both compare server-minted stamps against server-minted stamps: same clock, same format, and fixed-width ISO-UTC compares lexicographically exactly as it compares chronologically. No client clock ever participates in an ordering decision — the client's write-adoption logic (lastWriteAt, writeSettledAt, started >=) compares Date.now() only against other Date.now() values from the same machine.

Displaying — the only two places server time meets a viewer's eyes both handle zones deliberately. closedStamp renders tfin via getHours/getDate etc., i.e. the viewer's local wall clock (the comment says "in the viewer's local time" — that's the spec), and DST is free because the browser does that mapping. ago() subtracts Date.parse(iso) — zone-independent for ISO-with-Z — from the client clock, and the one place skew *could* show (a client behind the server seeing a bid "submitted -3s ago") is already floored to 0s with a comment saying exactly why.

The geo cache TTL is client-ISO vs client-now — self-consistent.

Three findings from the audit, all assessment, none fixed:

  1. The Closed line carries no zone marker. Two participants in different zones will see different wall-clock text for the same instant — "Closed 2026-07-16 13:01 Thu" vs "…16:01 Thu". That's inherent to the local-time spec and right for a screen; it only bites if someone screenshots the line into a group chat as if it were canonical. Your call whether that ever matters.
  1. The whole edifice rests on stamps staying TEXT in the sheet, and the armor has a known edge. The '@' plain-text format is applied at tab creation to getMaxRows() rows (1000). If a stamp cell ever escapes that — row 1001+, or someone hand-clearing formats — Sheets coerces the ISO string to a real date, and rows()'s String() then yields "Fri Jul 17 2026 18:23:45 GMT-0700 (Pacific Daylight Time)" in the *script's* timezone. I verified the nasty part empirically: that string sneaks past ingest's tfin.includes('T') assert — "GMT" and "Time" both contain a T — and it misorders lexicographically against ISO, so the standing-bid-at-or-before-tfin logic would silently misjudge rather than fail loudly. If you want the belt: tighten the assert to a real shape check (/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T/) so a coerced stamp crashes the ingest instead of rendering nonsense — one-line change plus a qual, on the anti-Postel doctrine. Say the word.
  1. Minor, already flagged in turn one: a legacy bid row with a blank tbid (the hand-written-row case the gas quals bless) makes ago('') return "NaNd", so the tooltip reads "bid submitted NaNd ago" — time-adjacent cosmetic on a tamper-only path.

Two questions — let me answer the format cliff properly, and actually test the ipwho.is theory from your machine (same public IP as your browser) before speculating:

Both answered — and the live probe just explained your 429 mystery rather neatly.

The format cliff, concretely

Google Sheets cells default to "Automatic" format, which means Sheets *interprets* whatever gets written: 007 becomes the number 7, MAR1 becomes March 1st, and an ISO stamp like 2026-07-18T22:01:33.510Z becomes a real datetime value. Code.gs defends against this — that's why a bid of "007" stays "007" — by setting the cells to plain-text (setNumberFormat('@')) when it first creates a tab. The catch: that armor is applied to getMaxRows() rows *at creation time*, and a fresh sheet's grid is 1000 rows. The bids tab is an append-only log across all auctions combined, so its row count only grows. If appendRow ever writes row 1001, that row sits outside the armored range — and if the cell is Automatic, the ISO stamp gets coerced into a datetime, which reads back through String() as "Fri Jul 18 2026 15:01:33 GMT-0700 (…)". That breaks the lexicographic standing-bid-versus-tfin comparison, and bid text like "007" quietly becomes "7". Since yesterday's STAMP_RE work the client at least refuses such a payload *loudly* instead of rendering nonsense — but that's still an outage starting at submission #1001.

The honest caveat: it's a *suspected* cliff. Sheets often inherits formatting from the row above when appendRow grows the grid, in which case row 1001 arrives pre-armored and this never fires. I didn't want to claim it as a confirmed bug without testing against real Sheets. The fix-shape if you want certainty: armor whole columns (or re-arm on growth) in tab(), plus a one-time live test — small Code.gs change, needs a deploy.

The ipwho.is 429s — probed live from this machine (your IP)

Findings: a plain request right now returns 200, success:true — and here's the good part — with cf-cache-status: HIT. Adding an Origin: https://tauction.dreev.es header (what your browser's CORS fetch sends) flips it to cf-cache-status: BYPASS: browser requests from the app bypass Cloudflare's cache and hit the counted, rate-limited API, while plain navigations often get free cached rides. That's why ipwho.is "works in your normal browser" while the app sees 429s — they're not even taking the same path.

As for why you *keep* seeing them: it's the failure-retry spiral. locate() only stamps its localStorage cache on success, so during any throttled window every page load retries and logs a fresh 429 to the console — and dev live-reload means a load per file save, which both sustains the spam and is what likely trips the burst limit in the first place. Each origin and browser profile has its own localStorage too (localhost:8000, tauction.dreev.es, your phone, every incognito window), so each needs one successful lookup to go quiet. A 4-request burst just now got all 200s, so your IP isn't currently exhausted — the 429s you see are transient throttling during exactly the sessions where you'd be looking at the console.

Recommendation: no fallback service. Geography is decoration by your own doctrine; a second geo provider is a new dependency and one more party seeing your users' IPs, to slightly improve tooltip garnish availability — a trade, not a Pareto move. Steady state with the day-cache is ~1 lookup per browser per day, which the free tier covers hundreds of times over. What *would* help is small and dependency-free: stamp the attempt, not just the success, so a failed lookup waits out a backoff (say an hour) instead of retrying on every load — that kills the console spam and the burst-limit feedback loop in one line-ish change, and the failure path isn't pinned by any qual, so it's free to change. Want me to do that one?

The format cliff, worked all the way to ground

The clearest way to say it, in three beats:

  1. Why armor exists. Sheets *interprets* anything written into a cell unless that cell is formatted plain-text. This app writes strings: bids like 007, stamps like 2026-07-18T22:01:33.510Z. In an interpreting cell, Sheets stores the number 7 and a real datetime — and reading those back gives "7" and "Fri Jul 18 2026 15:01:33 GMT-0700 (…)". The first corrupts bid text; the second breaks the lexicographic stamp ordering that decides which bid beat the gavel.
  2. The armor's extent. tab() applies plain-text format exactly once, at tab creation, to getMaxRows() rows — and a fresh sheet's grid is 1000 rows. Rows 1–1000 are safe forever. Think of it as a paint job applied to the parking lot as originally built.
  3. The cliff. The bids tab is an append-only log across *all* auctions, so it only grows. Writing row 1001 forces Sheets to first *grow the grid* — and whether newborn grid rows inherit the plain-text format from the rows above, or arrive in default interpreting mode, is the whole question.

What research settles: the Apps Script docs are silent, but the REST API underneath has exactly two grow primitives — insertDimension, which has an inheritFromBefore flag and *can* copy formatting from the row above, and appendDimension, which appends blank rows with default properties, no inheritance. Which one appendRow uses when it grows the grid is undocumented. Community evidence leans "no inheritance": there's an entire genre of workaround scripts and support threads about appended rows (Google Forms responses being the classic case) failing to keep the formatting of the rows above them. So the right posture is: treat the cliff as real — and even if today's behavior happened to inherit, it's undocumented behavior that could change underneath us, which is its own reason not to lean on it.

Urgency, measured against your live sheet (it's link-readable, so I counted): bids 17 rows, users 11, auctions 8. The fastest-growing tab is ~983 submissions from the edge — years away at current usage — and since the STAMP_RE work, falling off it would be a loud "bad state shape" banner, not silent corruption.

  • The belt (recommended): make the question moot. A tiny Code.gs helper: appendRow, then re-apply '@' to the just-written row and re-set the same values — the rewrite un-coerces anything a transiently-interpreting cell mangled, all inside the script lock so no reader ever sees the intermediate. Execution times: measured, and yes, there's real headroom

Live measurement: a bare state GET takes 1.6–3.0s (three probes). The anatomy explains it — every rows(xTab()) costs ~3 service calls (openById + getSheetByName + the data read), and the code re-fetches with abandon. A single placeBid currently makes roughly 35–40 Sheets calls: full getState for the revealed-guard (~9–12), then the users tab read *four separate times* (deviceOf, ensureSeat, setDeviceID), the auctions tab twice, a second full getState for the response payload, and — the standout — repaintBids re-painting every bid row of the auction on every single bid, an O(N) write parade that grows as the auction goes on. And since every write holds the script lock for its whole call parade, concurrent bidders queue behind ~2s each — lock hold time is the real multi-bidder cost.

The arrival edge

The three one-shot latches — caretPlaced, descModeSet, and wasRevealed's null sentinel — turned out to all fire on the *same event*: the first adopted snapshot, cached or live. So they're now one named thing: adopted, the arrival edge. The caret lands on the arrival render, the description picks its mode on the arrival render, and fanfare belongs only to a *witnessed* sealed→revealed flip — a latecomer's arrival sets the baseline silently. switchAuction resets one bit instead of three, and the null-sentinel pattern is gone (wasRevealed is a plain boolean now).

Per the refactor discipline, the net went up before the wire moved: two characterization pins for arrival behaviors that were previously unpinned — a stale-unrevealed cache makes your arrival a *witnessed* reveal (fanfare and money play, at the strike's usual beat), and a cache-painted arrival seats the caret before the live fetch even lands. Both were green against the old code, stayed green through the fold, and one of them caught its own timing bug on the way in (asserting confetti before the 850ms strike), which is exactly the kind of thing I now distrust by default after yesterday's tautology sweep.

The commit pulse (your ruling: brief flash)

The instant a gesture queues a write, the field it happened in glows the shimmer green once and fades (~0.6s) — the outgoing twin of the incoming shimmer: sweep means *their news arrived*, glow means *yours is away*. It fires in five places: the auction name (only when the name actually takes — a gate refusal stays pulseless beside its banner), the + row (any add or seat-claim), the bid editor (at submit, not at settle), renames (a same-name snap-back doesn't pulse), and the description card. The sticky banner (your ruling: sticky + ×)

The 5-second self-destruct is deleted. A banner now leaves exactly three ways: its own × (new, quiet, inked like the message), a newer banner replacing it, or a later *successful* settle retiring it — stale bad news doesn't outlive the problem it reported, while the durable signal (the red field) stays. The dead-end sign's special "sticky" status is gone because *all* banners are sticky now; what remains of that function is just the markup-vs-text distinction, renamed linkBanner.

good idea. what are the pros and cons of polling in the background?
09:11 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 57s

Let me check the actual poll cadence first so the numbers are right.

Here's my honest read, for this app specifically (5s poll, Apps Script backend).

Pros

  • The tab-title payoff completes: 🔒→🎉 happens in the tab bar while you're elsewhere, which is exactly when you'd want it — "waiting on the gavel" is the one state where you've parked the tab and moved on.
  • Returning to a tab shows current truth instead of up-to-5s-stale (though there's a much cheaper way to get this one — see below).
  • Fresher state in forgotten tabs means fewer stale-roster races losing to the server (the loud refusals Sol just added would fire less often).

Cons

  • The backend is quota-bound and executes as you. Every poll is a doGet execution against your account's Apps Script quotas — shared across all visitors, roughly 0.5–2s of runtime each. One tab left open 24h at 5s cadence is ~17,000 requests and hours of accumulated runtime per day. Tabs get forgotten; that cost is perpetual and multiplies per tab, and dead tabs' polls compete with live bidders' writes for the 30-simultaneous-executions ceiling and the script lock during actual games.
  • Browsers won't actually let you poll at 5s in the background. Chrome's intensive throttling clamps background timers to about once per minute after a few minutes; Safari and mobile browsers freeze or discard background pages outright (and the PWA-on-a-phone case — your hallway audience — is the most aggressively frozen of all). So the honest deliverable isn't "flips within 5s," it's "flips within a minute, sometimes, on desktop." A feature that silently degrades like that is anti-Postel-adjacent: it makes a promise the platform won't keep.
  • Battery and radio cost on phones, for a payoff (one bit: revealed or not) that arrives at most once per auction's lifetime. Continuous cost, rare benefit.

The middle path that gets most of the value for ~none of the cost: refresh once on visibilitychange → visible. No background traffic at all, but the moment you click back to a tab it's current immediately instead of waiting out the interval. That kills the practical staleness complaint; the only thing it doesn't deliver is the 🎉 flipping while the tab is unfocused. If you wanted that too, the bounded version is: poll in the background *only* while the auction is hot (all bids in, awaiting reveal) at the browser's throttled cadence — the flip lands within a minute during the only window it can happen, and forgotten tabs of finished or idle auctions stay silent. That costs one condition, which per house rules I'd want your ruling on anyway.

My recommendation: visibilitychange refresh yes, unconditional background polling no. The hot-window variant is defensible if the tab-bar reveal moment matters to you enough to spend a branch on it.

what do you mean "the only window it can happen"? if not everyone has bid, but then they do bid, how do we know that without polling?
09:36 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 58s

You're right, and that's a real hole in what I proposed — thanks for pressing on it. The gate I described evaluates on the tab's *last-seen* state, and a backgrounded tab's knowledge freezes at its final visible poll. So if bids were still missing when you switched away, the tab sits in "not hot, don't poll" — and since not-polling is exactly what keeps it ignorant, it never learns the last bid landed, never enters the "hot window," and never sees the reveal. The gate only works in the case where everyone had already bid before you backgrounded the tab. That's the least common waiting scenario, not the main one — usually *you've* bid and you're waiting on stragglers, which is precisely the state my gate would go blind in.

The general principle I tripped over: a background-polling gate has to fail open, not closed. If the gate errs toward polling, one wasted poll discovers the truth and self-corrects. If it errs toward silence, the blindness is self-perpetuating, because polling is the only way the gate's own inputs get refreshed.

That asymmetry is also why there's exactly one clean state-based gate available: revealed. It's a one-way latch, and the tab learns it *by* polling — so "poll in background unless revealed" errs only on the polling side (a revealed-elsewhere tab polls once more, sees the latch, and goes permanently quiet). The corrected menu is really just:

  1. No background polling — the title updates next time you look (plus a visibilitychange refresh so "next time you look" is instant). Zero background cost, no reveal-while-away flip.
  2. Poll in background whenever unrevealed, stopping forever at reveal. This is the coherent version of what I was reaching for. The browser throttles it to roughly once a minute on desktop and freezes it on mobile regardless, so the real cost is ~1,400 requests/day per *abandoned unrevealed* desktop tab — the finished-auction tabs, which are the ones people most often leave open forever, cost nothing after their one discovery poll.
  3. Time-decay schemes (poll for a while after backgrounding, then give up) — bounds the abandoned-tab cost but adds machinery and a mushy promise ("flips if it happens within an hour"). I'd rule it out on house style alone.

So the honest trade is between 1 and 2, and it's the question of whether the 🎉-while-away flip is worth ~1/min from every open unrevealed tab. My lean is still 1 — the flip is a nicety, the visibilitychange refresh captures most of the felt value, and the backend runs on your quota — but 2 is now the version I'd defend if you want the tab bar to announce the gavel.

The central omission is emerging: the current title has only “sealed” and “revealed,” while the auction itself has a third, operationally important state—“all bids are in; someone must press reveal.” I’m checking the exact state derivation and whether background reads carry that signal cleanly.

Fable fixed the self-blinding “hot window” mistake, but it still treats a background poll as if it only updates the title. In this app it does much more.

  1. A hidden poll would perform a full render.

[refresh()](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:273) calls ingest() and render(). If reveal arrives while hidden, that:

  • Consumes the one-shot gavel/confetti ceremony offscreen via [celebrate()](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:473).
  • Consumes incoming-bid shimmers.
  • Can disable a focused dirty bid/name field, whose blur handler may then submit the draft after the gavel and produce an error ([bid blur](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:741), [reveal disabling](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:816)).
  • Can create a sticky network-error banner while hidden; later successful reads do not clear it.

A hidden poll therefore needs a title-only/pending-state path, or an explicit ruling that hidden tabs count as witnessing the reveal.

  1. It misses the state that actually calls the user back.

There are three states, not two:

waiting → ready for someone to reveal → revealed

Reveal is deliberately manual ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:438)), and readiness is already derived separately ([app.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:480)). But the title stays 🔒 for both waiting and ready ([stringles.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/stringles.js:51)). Background polling can learn that the last bid arrived yet communicate nothing. The first product question is whether the away-signal means “come back and reveal” or “someone revealed.” If it is the former, the title needs a third state.

  1. Its timer arithmetic is Chrome-specific.

Chrome only moves chained timers to approximately once per minute after more than five minutes hidden and under additional conditions. Firefox Desktop’s documented minimum is one second, so tauction’s five-second interval may remain a five-second interval—about 17,000 calls/day. Chrome’s policy, cross-browser timer behavior.

If background polling is chosen, tauction should request an explicit coarse hidden cadence, such as 60 seconds, rather than outsourcing its traffic ceiling to browser heuristics.

  1. The backend analysis is partly wrong.

State GETs do not acquire the script lock; only mutations do ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:128)). Polls consume execution and Sheets capacity, but do not “compete for the script lock.” Because reads are unlocked, they can instead observe intermediate states during multi-write mutations.

Also, every poll reads and scans the complete auctions, users, and append-only bids tabs ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:265)). Cost therefore grows with all historical activity. The repository’s own live measurement says 1.6–3.0 seconds for a bare state GET ([gas-quals.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/quals/gas-quals.js:779)), not Fable’s 0.5–2 seconds.

The general quota concern is valid, but Google’s published 90-minute/6-hour daily runtime quota is specifically trigger runtime; the documented general limits include 30 simultaneous executions per user and 1,000 per script. Apps Script quotas.

  1. “Immediate on visibilitychange” overpromises.

It would start revalidation immediately, but the old controls remain actionable until the request finishes. Furthermore, [refresh()](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:273) silently refuses while another fetch is active, has no timeout, and queues no refire. Preventing stale-return races would also require visibly graying/locking the ledger until catch-up completes.

Recommendation: retain no hidden polling if the goal is merely freshness on return; add visibility-triggered revalidation and gray the stale UI. If the tab itself should signal progress while away, use an explicit slow hidden cadence, add the ready state to the title, update only title/pending state while hidden, and defer the full render and ceremony until visible. “Stop at reveal” should apply only to hidden polling, since descriptions remain editable after reveal. No files changed.

The principled case, per the links:

  • Anti-Postel doesn't apply — it's about rejecting malformed *input*. This input is well-formed and the requested post-condition ("alice is on the roster") already holds. Reporting failure for a satisfied request is the actual falsehood; that's your complaint exactly.

Let me trace the actual mechanics before diagnosing — the device id minting, the claim flow, and how each browser decides what bid text to show.

Traced it. Nothing is fubar in the data — the sheet has exactly one standing bid for bob (the log is append-only; the latest row at reveal wins). What's fubar is that both browsers *display* a different "bob's bid," and at most one of them is telling the truth. Here's the full chain:

The deviceID guess is wrong, in a good way. Each browser profile mints crypto.randomUUID() into localStorage on first load ([app.js:155-158](app.js#L155-L158)) — incognito has separate storage, so it has its *own* uuid. The architecture is already what you describe as right. That's also why the two-normal-tabs test behaves: two tabs of one profile are literally one device — same uuid, same tauction-pids, same tauction-mybids — so an edit in one tab is read back by the other on its next poll.

The takeover is not a malfunction — it's the faire ruling. Until 2026-07-21 the server refused a claim on a seat held by another device (ERROR1304 seatHeldCopy). That lock was deliberately deleted in the faire fix, because Safari re-minted her uuid and her own seat refused her: claims became "consistency markers, not auth — a tap on a taken star TAKES the seat, last write wins" ([Code.gs:631-638](apps-script/Code.gs#L631-L638), [app.js:980-987](app.js#L980-L987)). Your expectata is exactly the pre-faire behavior; the regression is that ruling's known cost surfacing.

Why each window sees its own bid. Sealed bid text never leaves the server, so each browser renders a bid it placed from its own tauction-mybids memory ([app.js:574-587](app.js#L574-L587)) — "you always see the bids your own browser placed." That rule is only truthful while one browser sits in a seat. After incognito takes bob and re-bids, the normal window is unseated (a rival's registered claim demotes mypid() to nobody, [app.js:562-567](app.js#L562-L567)), and bob's row becomes a card showing the normal window's *superseded* text — stamp and stack sheets update, but the words silently stay stale. Incognito's editor shows its own text. Two windows, two "bob's bids," one lie.

Two ways out, and they pull against each other:

  1. Bid protects its seat from claims too — the server already refuses removing a bidder; extend the same refusal to claiming a seat that has a bid. Simple, matches your expectata. Cost: re-creates a slice of faire — a bidder whose localStorage evaporates (Safari ITP does this) can never re-enter their own seat to re-bid, and there's no escape hatch short of the claim tokens the spec already rejected.
  2. Keep takeovers, stop the display lying — stamp the local bid memory with bcount at placement; when the seat's current bcount no longer matches, this browser's text is superseded, so render the masked decoy like any other sealed bid (and optionally banner the unseating instead of demoting silently). Honor system intact, faire intact, and every window shows something true.

Which way do you want it?

10:48 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m8s

I think the faire ruling was half right, and the half that's wrong isn't the half you're pointing at.

The claim lock that refused faire wasn't anti-Postel virtue — it was an if-statement enforcing a credential the system doesn't have. A deviceID is an unstable uuid (Safari purges localStorage on its own schedule) that sits in a link-visible sheet, so the lock couldn't stop anyone acting in bad faith — they can read the uuid right out of the sheet and send it. A lock that can't stop adversaries but permanently strands honest users with cleared storage is theater, and "clearer errors" can't rescue it: the clearest possible message to faire would still have been a refusal with no path forward, because her old uuid was gone from the universe. There's no wording that fixes a dead end. Deleting that lock was the anti-magic move — one rule (last write wins), no recovery flows, no escape hatches, consistent with "honor system throughout" everywhere else in the app.

What the ruling got wrong is that it deleted the refusal without adding the loudness. Anti-Postel doesn't demand the server refuse things; it demands nothing fail *silently*. Two silences slipped through:

  1. The display lies. The unseated window keeps rendering its cached text as if it were bob's standing bid. That's Postel-style tolerance of divergence — the client "helpfully" shows what it remembers instead of admitting it no longer knows. The echo design is the anti-Postel fix: render only what the server attests, mask the rest. Notably, this is needed under *either* claim policy — even if you restored a lock, the API takes bids by pid (honor system), so a rival re-bid and a stale cache stay representable. The lock doesn't subsume it.
  2. The unseating is mute. When a rival claim demotes you, your editor quietly becomes a card mid-session. That deserves a banner in the unseated window — the event announced, not refused.

So my actual position: takeovers stay legal (the lock was fake anyway), the display becomes incapable of lying (echo, cache deleted), and the takeover becomes loud (banner for the unseated, and the taken star's tip already names the claimant's rig for the taker). Faire under this regime: no refusals, and if someone re-bids her seat while she's away, she comes back to a masked card and a banner instead of a phantom of her old bid.

The one real fork left is whether you want *bid finality per device* — "once bob bids from browser X, only browser X may revise it." That's a product stance, not an engineering one, and it contradicts "everything stays editable, honor system" as written. If you want it anyway, it's the refuse-claims-on-bid-seats variant, plus the echo fix regardless. Do you?

10:53 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 50s

Yes — that's exactly the problem, and it's worth walking through concretely because the failure is sneaky.

What the server calls a "device" is really *a uuid in one browser profile's localStorage*. That identity is guaranteed by nothing. Safari's tracking prevention deletes a site's script-writable storage after about a week of not interacting with the site; private windows shed it at close; people clear site data; and the same human on phone-plus-laptop is two "devices" from birth. So under finality-per-device, here is the timeline for a completely honest bob:

  • Monday: bob bids from his iPhone (uuid A recorded as the bid's owner).
  • The following week: Safari quietly purges the site's storage.
  • Friday, before the reveal: bob comes back to fix a typo in his bid. His browser mints uuid B, presents it, and the server refuses him — he *is* the stranger now. There is no error message that helps, because there's nothing he can present; uuid A no longer exists anywhere except the sheet. His typo is final. That's faire's lockout, relocated from claims to bids.

And now the other leg: that same Friday, anyone at all can open the link-visible sheet, read uuid A out of the bids row, and POST a "revision" carrying it. Accepted. So the lock refuses the person it was built for and admits the person it was built against. You'd pay the stranding cost and receive no finality in return — it's theater with casualties.

Could the id be made durable and secret so the lock becomes real? That's the token design your own spec already rejected, and the rejection was correct: a secret token *also* lives in localStorage, so Safari eats it too, and durable identity that survives storage loss means accounts and recovery flows — the complexity cliff this app exists to stay off of. The honest summary is: you can't have finality per device, because there is no device. There's only "person," and persons have no credentials here — by design, everywhere: roster edits, renames, and the reveal button are all already anyone-may-act, honor-system, last-write-wins.

So the thing you're reaching for with finality — "nobody should quietly bid over bob from another browser" — is real, but the deliverable version of it is *quietly*, not *nobody*: the taken star already announces itself and names the claimant's rig before the tap; the unseated window should get a banner instead of a silent demotion; and the superseded browser should show a masked card instead of a phantom of its old text. Visible, attributable, socially enforceable — the same security model as the rest of the app, made loud where it's currently mute.

Shall I build that — the per-device echo (cache deleted), the unseat banner, quals first?

I’ll compare Fable’s latest recommendation against the repository state and the governing principles in AGENTS.md, then report whether it is technically sound and Pareto-safe.

The disputed point has two separable parts: the local fix for stale bid display, and Fable’s claim that durable per-device finality is impossible under this app’s honor-system architecture. I’m checking both against the actual state and bid paths.

Only partly. The diagnosis is correct; the recommendation is not clearly correct.

  • The bug is the unversioned tauction-mybids cache: fresh server metadata can coexist with superseded local text ([app.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/app.js:574)).
  • “Finality per device is impossible” is too strong. The UUID is not authentication, but it can still prevent accidental cross-browser overwrites. Locking bid-bearing seats versus permitting recovery after storage loss is a real PDP tradeoff, not a technical conclusion.
  • Fable’s echo design would make sealed bids queryable: state currently publishes every claimant’s raw device ID ([Code.gs](/Users/dreeves/lab/tauction/apps-script/Code.gs:423)). Replaying those IDs could retrieve the corresponding bids. It also requires schema migration and viewer-ID plumbing through every response—not merely “one column and one filter.”
  • Safari loss is real, but the precise rule is seven days of Safari use without site interaction; home-screen apps are exempt. Faire’s Safari explanation was never established as the actual cause. WebKit documentation

The narrower recommendation is:

  1. Key locally known bid text by the server’s existing (pid, bcount, tmod) version; if the current version has no matching text, mask it. No schema change or bid oracle.
  2. Separately decide whether “a bid protects its seat.” Bidless takeovers would still solve Faire’s case; bid-bearing seats would refuse rival claims, matching test0951. The cost is lockout if that browser loses storage.
  3. Do not bundle an unseat banner into this fix. It is separate behavior, requires explicit approval, and any new copy requires Latin plus the prescribed TODO.

Two answers.

Faire: agreed, we don't know. The precise ITP rule (7 days of *Safari use* without visiting the site; home-screen apps exempt) makes a wipe less likely than the mundane causes: she first opened the link in an in-app webview (Messages/Slack) and later in real Safari, or a private window, or her other device — every one of which is "same human, new uuid." Server-side these are indistinguishable from a wipe, so the etiology is unrecoverable now. It also doesn't matter: deleting the claim lock fixed the whole class, cause-agnostically. The ruling survives our ignorance.

Remove code and Pareto-dominate: no — and I can say why structurally. Pick two of three: (a) sealed text never leaves the server pre-reveal (the echo violated this — replayable ids), (b) your browser always shows the bid it placed (your own help copy, and your two-tab expectata), (c) no client-side bid memory. Given (a) and (b), memory must exist, and memory that rivals can supersede needs a freshness bit. The only genuine code-removal on the table was deleting the cache, which sacrifices (b) — a feature regression, not Pareto.

The floor is therefore Sol's stamp, and it's smaller than Sol sized it: every write handler already returns a full state snapshot as its ack ([Code.gs:602-607](apps-script/Code.gs#L602-L607) pattern), so placeBid can stamp its memory with the acked tmod and knownBids() includes text only when the stamp still matches the seat's current tmod. 14:57 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 59s

Threat model of the echo under a locked-down sheet:

Adversary: any participant, or anyone they forward the URL to — the web app must stay access-Anyone (that's the CORS-simple fetch model), so the auction URL *is* the access credential.

Vector: the state response hands every client the claims map as raw pid → deviceID ([Code.gs:428-434](apps-script/Code.gs#L428-L434)) — it's how rival stars render as taken. Under echo, a deviceID becomes a key that unlocks sealed text. So: call state once, harvest every claimant's id, replay each one, read every standing bid.

Effort: DevTools or curl. No exploit, no race, no luck.

Impact: complete collapse of sealing — the one thing the app exists to provide. And it's the worst kind: the snoop reads everyone, then bids with perfect information. Not a privacy leak; a rigged auction.

Detectability: zero. Reads are silent, the victims never learn, and nothing in the sheet records that it happened.

The categorical difference from the status quo: today (sheet locked) there is *no secret whose theft matters* — sealed text lives only server-side, state responses carry text only post-reveal, and deviceIDs open no doors because they were designed as consistency markers, not credentials. The echo's sin isn't "text on the wire" per se — it's minting a credential out of an identifier the app already publishes. A repurposed-public-id key is pre-stolen.

Could the echo be repaired? Yes: publish only hashes in the claims map (clients compare the hash of their own uuid), keep raw ids request-side; a 122-bit uuid is then an unguessable bearer secret. But notice what that is — the secret-token architecture your spec already rejected, arriving through the back door, with all its properties: localStorage loss silently revokes the credential, shared devices hold it, and you're now curating a secret-vs-published split forever. All to delete a small cache that the stamp fix makes truthful in three lines while keeping the invariant that makes the whole API unprivileged.

One more consequence of your assumption: once the sheet is locked, the "sealing is honor-system" caveat in the help copy stops being true — the invariant becomes the actual security boundary, which raises the price of ever violating it later. Worth a line in AGENTS.md's scratchpad when we get there.

Still ready to build the stamp fix on your word.

no, we need to close that hole. so the choices are (a) transmit hashes of the sealed bids, or (b) trust the client to keep track of its own bid until reveal. is that right?
17:08 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 46s

Not quite — (a) is a trap, and (b) as stated is the current bug.

(a) Hashes of sealed bids leak the bids. Bid texts are tiny, low-entropy strings — "42", "three tacos", "$100". Anyone holding the hash enumerates plausible bids offline until one matches; numeric bids fall in microseconds. Salting doesn't help: a public salt lets the attacker enumerate with it, a secret salt means the client can't verify either. When the message space is small, any derivative of the text *is* the text. The codebase already knows this principle — it's why the mask is a constant decoy rather than a blur of the real bid ([app.js:23-25](app.js#L23-L25)).

(b) Trusting the client's memory is the status quo — and untrusted-freshness memory is exactly what lied in test0951.

The missing option is (b) plus a freshness check against metadata that's *already public and not derived from the text*: the seat's submission counter. bcount bumps once per submission and every write ack returns a fresh state snapshot, so the client stores {text, bcount} at placement and knownBids() shows the text only while the seat's current bcount still equals the stored one. A rival re-bid bumps the counter → mismatch → decoy. Your own re-bid re-stamps → still shown. Two tabs share the memory → both show edits, as you expect. (bcount over tmod because it's collision-free by construction; timestamps can tie.)

Nothing text-derived ever crosses the wire, so the hole you're closing stays closed, and the client is trusted only with what it already knows — its own words, displayed only while they're still the standing bid.

I treated the omission as intent, preserved the exception, and *flagged* it — twice — as "the one buttonless field, say the word." Each edit was locally faithful to a ruling; nobody re-derived the whole gesture table after the law changed. That's the whack-a-mole mechanism itself: exceptions outliving the reasons that justified them, and a buried flag treated as ratification.

Is the context too long? Not as a retrieval problem — I had every fact, including my own flag. It's long enough that a flagged-but-unanswered question scrolls out of *your* view, though, and I wrongly treated your silence about it as a decision. The discipline failure is what let that matter, and I've written it into memory as its own rule: after any consistency ruling, re-derive the entire table it governs and kill or re-justify every standing exception aloud — flags aren't decisions.

The banner. It's not Firefox-specific — I reproduced it identically in real Firefox *and* Chrome (puppeteer against serve.py + fake-gas). The trigger just happens to live in your Firefox's localStorage:

  1. Some past Firefox session left the description editor dirty — one uncommitted keystroke suffices, since blur commits nothing. That draft is persisted in tauction-drafts:<aname> and kept forever ([app.js:501](app.js#L501)).
  2. Since then the blurb was edited from another browser, so tblurb moved past what that Firefox last saw.
  3. On the next Firefox load, [restoreDrafts](app.js#L525) hands the stale draft back at the arrival edge, making the editor dirty; when the live snapshot lands, [renderDesc's dirty branch](app.js#L570) sees a moved tblurb and banners simulEditsBanner.
  4. Meanwhile the card is in viewing mode (blurb non-empty at arrival), and [style.css:209](style.css#L209) hides the editor — so the dirty draft is invisible. Banner, red ring on a display:none field, no visible cause.

To confirm in your Firefox, on the auction page: localStorage.getItem('tauction-drafts:' + location.pathname.slice(1)). To purge: ✎ (the stale draft becomes visible), then Escape. The warn-and-rebase is by design for a foreign edit landing mid-edit; firing it at the arrival edge for a weeks-old invisible draft is the same code path reading as noise.

Minutes to load. Fresh-profile headless Firefox on this machine: production load event 480ms, live snapshot adopted 2.8s; local serve.py 160ms. So the slowness is in your Firefox profile or its network path (extension, ETP strict, DoH, HTTP/3), not the app's assets or code. But the app amplifies it: the state fetch has no timeout, and the refreshing latch ([app.js:386](app.js#L386)) makes every 5s poll and the tab-return refresh early-return while a request is in flight — one hung connection silently wedges *all* polling for as long as Firefox holds the socket, with the ledger grayed under the gavel the whole time. And when the wedge finally clears, the first adopted snapshot is exactly the one that cries simultaneous-edits — the two symptoms chained in the order your report describes.

One question, since only you can observe the wedge: next time it's slow-loading in Firefox, is the console silent (a hung fetch — the latch wedge) or repeating transport warnings every few seconds (fast-failing fetches — something in the profile blocking script.google.com)?

Assessments on all five, grounded in the code. No changes made yet.

1. Mobile = bigger? Mostly yes. There are currently zero width breakpoints in style.css — one layout for everything. Two "bigger" moves carry most of the value: (a) form fields are 0.85rem = 13.6px ([style.css:215](style.css#L215)); anything under 16px makes iOS Safari zoom-jump on focus, which alone makes a page feel broken on a phone — bump inputs/textareas to 16px; (b) tap targets: the star is 24×32px ([style.css:985](style.css#L985)), the × similar, and SAVE/SUBMIT text is 0.6rem ≈ 10px ([style.css:318](style.css#L318)) against the ~44px Apple/Android guideline — grow hit areas via padding, not necessarily glyphs. The one thing bigger can't fix is the in-field buttons colliding with text on narrow widths, which is item 2. The PHONE/NARROW story quals fence any of this.

2. Buttons inside the field. Agree. Inside-placement steals typing width (three separate padding-right compensations exist) and puts a tiny target next to the blurb's resize grip. The standard pattern is a right-aligned button row *below* the field, shown while hot — the cost is a row-height reflow when a field goes hot, which the current overlay avoids. I lean below-the-field; it also gives item 3 a free home.

3. Abandon button. The gesture exists: ✎ (draft becomes visible and focused), then Escape — reverts to the rebased server truth and deletes the draft. Two things worth knowing before deciding: reloading does *not* abandon — the draft store survives reloads by design, so the banner's "reload the page" advice leaves the draft lurking dirty in the hidden editor, primed to re-cry at the next foreign edit (that's exactly the Firefox-report mechanism). And touch keyboards have no Escape, so mobile users currently can't abandon at all. As a banner-button: not worth it. As a CANCEL beside SAVE if item 2 moves buttons below fields: nearly free, and it fixes the mobile gap.

4. Gavel audit. Research done — here's the answer, no code yet.

What the literature says. Two principles bear directly. First, NN/g's progress-indicator research: looped animations are for 2–10 second waits; under ~1 second they're distracting flicker (their video guidance is the 1s floor). Apps Script round trips are 0.5–2s, so tauction's writes sit mostly *below* the zone where a spinner earns its keep at all — which is what the 0.3s appearance delay already encodes. Second, Material's guideline (same in M2): placement communicates scope — an indicator attached to a container says "this item is busy, the rest of the UI is usable"; a screen-level indicator says "the whole screen is loading." The corollary convention everywhere (Google Docs' "Saving…", the browser tab spinner): *optimistic background saves get a small fixed status indicator, never a page-scope one*, because nothing is actually blocked.

Applied here. A big whole-page gavel would say "wait — the page is busy" at the exact moments the app is proudly *not* busy: every write is optimistic and everything stays interactive. It would also throb over the words you're mid-typing (commits happen while your eyes are at a field), and — the app-specific argument — the giant center-stage gavel is currently *reserved vocabulary*: it appears once, dramatically, at the reveal ceremony. Spending it on every roster nudge dilutes the one theatrical moment the app has. Could a translucent watermark version be made to look good? Probably yes, aesthetically. But it would look good while saying the wrong thing.

The anti-magic reading. It cuts the same way, and it's the strongest argument for the singleton *regardless* of size: one gavel element, shown iff writesPending > 0, flipped at the existing startWrite/settleWrite chokepoint. That deletes miniGavel(), the per-tile gavel appends, the per-op host thunks, and all four animation selector groups — strictly fewer code paths than today. Taken to its clean end, the pending-row gray dies with them (optimistic-UI practice: successful background writes need no pending mark; failures already banner loudly and refresh), leaving exactly two signals in the whole app: the table gray meaning "this *picture* may be stale" (arrival, outage, probe, reveal) and the one gavel meaning "talking to the server." Placement is then a one-line CSS choice — corner vs. center changes zero code structure.

Recommendation: the singleton at a fixed corner of the column (by share/help), modest size, 0.3s-delayed — the researched convention for background saves — keeping the giant gavel exclusively for the ceremony. If you want to see the big translucent center version anyway, it's the same one CSS block and a screenshot away.

Corner, or show you the big one first?

12:45 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 2m32s · 2m38s wall-clock time

Gathered three more rounds — and the answer did become clear, just not between the two options I offered. Both die.

Your instinct about the corner is right, but inverted. The question isn't whether a corner spinner is noticeable enough — it's that it's noticeable in the wrong way. Peripheral vision is motion-tuned (the rod-dominated retina detects movement best off-center; peripheral motion triggers an involuntary, bottom-up attention shift), and NN/g's guidance is blunt about the consequence: animated elements in the periphery unrelated to the current task are hard to *stop* attending to and degrade the experience. A gavel hammering in the corner during every write wouldn't be too subtle — it would yank your eye away from the field you're typing in, several times a session.

And why you haven't seen it on other websites: because polished products with optimistic background writes — Trello, Figma, Linear, Instagram — show *nothing at all* while a write is in flight. The optimistic-UI school: for low-risk, likely-to-succeed writes, paint the result instantly and indicate only *failures*. Where a persistent indicator exists (Google Docs), it's a calm non-animated text chip — "Saving…/Saved" — and it exists for close-the-tab data-loss anxiety in document editors, not as activity display.

Here's the convergence, and it's the anti-magic answer too: tauction already has every piece the no-spinner school requires. The commit pulse flashes the field the instant a write queues (your 2026-07-19 ruling — feedback *at* the point of attention, exactly the "subtle, brief, task-relevant" animation NN/g endorses); failures banner loudly in the server's words with a recovery refresh; drafts survive the tab, so even an in-flight bid killed by a closing tab comes back as a draft. The busy gavels for writes are redundant with all three. So: no gavel for writes at all. Delete the row minis, the desc mini, the bid-volley mini, and the host-thunk plumbing. The one big gavel over the BIDS table survives for the states where the *picture* is genuinely untrusted — arrival, transport failure, the name probe, the reveal — which is Material-correct region scoping, and the ceremony keeps its giant strike undiluted. At most one gavel can ever spin, by construction, and the diff is pure deletion.

What you'd be giving up: the hammering gavel as everyday charm — it would appear only on page load, outages, and reveals. The one functional nuance lost is the bid-volley mini, whose job the grayed SUBMIT (holding words already on the wire) quietly covers.

Adopt no-spinner-for-writes?

Sources: NN/g — The Role of Animation and Motion in UX, NN/g — Animation for Attention and Comprehension, Progress — Peripheral Vision Drives User Attention, Smashing — True Lies of Optimistic User Interfaces, Smashing — Local-First Architecture, UI-Patterns — Autosave, NN/g — Progress Indicators, Material 3 — Progress Indicators.

1 — The audit. What it was: not technically overlap but zero-gap abutment — the breathing margin rode .hot .gorow only, and the landing's always-visible Go is the app's one *cold* visible button row, so it sat flush on the field's border. Why I kept missing this class of bug, layer by layer: the jsdom suite does no layout at all, so ~480 assertions are geometry-blind by construction; the story-suite geometry checks assert *relations I hypothesized* with tolerances chosen to make them decidable — my "below its field" predicate was top >= bottom − 0.5, which classifies *flush* as *below*; screenshots exist only for states a story explicitly shoots, and when I changed the resting landing page I never added a shot of the resting landing page; and my eyeballing reviews new screenshots, not the state × viewport matrix. The pattern across all three incidents (phone SUBMIT blanket, cover-below eating the star click, this): point asserts catch anticipated failures; geometry bugs live in unanticipated states. The structural remedy is an invariant: a layout auditor now sweeps every pair of visible interactive elements and demands 2px of daylight — no overlap, no abutment — exempting ancestor chains, the z-ladder's declared floaters, and dialogs. Can you do deep research on web design with the goal of predicting the first complaint a professional web designer would have about this app?
00:35 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m55s · 2m6s wall-clock time

Prediction, grounded in the app's measured type and the critique literature: the first complaint is the type scale — "your reading text is 13–14px and your action buttons are under 10px, on desktop, in a monospace face."

The reasoning chain. Design-review first impressions form pre-verbally from type, structure, and color (the 50ms studies; structure, spacing, text quantity, and fonts dominate the snap judgment) — and when a professional then verbalizes, the canonical checklist starts at body text: Butterick's four priorities are point size, line spacing, line length, font, with a stated web floor of 15–25px for text meant to be read. The app's reading surfaces — names, bids, the description — sit at 13.6px on desktop, and SAVE/SUBMIT are 9.6px bold uppercase. Sub-floor body text plus micro-labels on the *primary actions* is exactly the "too small to read" that tops the mistake lists (NN/g's top-10; IxDF's common mistakes). The irony a designer would enjoy pointing out: the coarse-pointer media query already fixes all of this for phones — the desktop is now the under-typeset platform.

The monospace face itself is where the complaint would *start* but probably not where it would stick. Butterick is categorical — "in standard body text, there are no good reasons to use monospaced fonts" — so expect it named in the first breath. But the app has a coherent identity (graph-paper dot grid, drawn gavel, terminal register) and intentional-looking system aesthetics survive critique; deliberate mono at a *generous size* reads as a choice, mono at 13.6px reads as a default nobody questioned.

Runners-up, in predicted order: (2) the whisper-text contrast — the ★-legend and footer are 11.2px at 75%-alpha of an already-muted gray, a double reduction that fails WCAG for text that size; (3) the app now speaks two design languages — a LaTeX paper inside a terminal — which a systems-minded designer would flag as unresolved, though defenders would call the dialog a document and the app a tool; (4) the unnamed-state gray at 0.45 opacity dims *text* below readability rather than just de-emphasizing it.

No changes made — this was the prediction. The cheapest counter to the predicted complaint, if wanted later: desktop reading text 0.85rem → 1rem and the .go labels up a notch, which is the same one-notch move the phone already got.

How exactly does it work if two people try to submit changes to the blurb at the same time?
13:09 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 52s · 58s wall-clock time

(The suite run from the copy-split is still blocked by the harness's shell restriction — npm run sync-404 && npm run quals remains the pending verification.)

The mechanism, end to end — it's the wikis' mid-air-collision model, adopted 2026-07-28:

The token. Every blurb version carries an opaque token, tblurb (ISO stamp plus a random tail, so two writes in the same millisecond can't share one). When the editor syncs cleanly from a snapshot, it records that token as dataset.base — the version the edit *started from*. While the editor is dirty or focused, renders leave it completely alone (words and base both), so a foreign save landing mid-composition changes nothing visible and warns nobody.

The save. SAVE paints the rendered pane immediately (optimistic) and POSTs describe{blurb, base}. Server-side, all writes go through one script lock, so two "simultaneous" submissions are serialized in lock-acquisition order. Inside the lock, describe compares the request's base to the current token — the *verdict comes before any write*: match → store the blurb, mint a fresh token, return the new state; mismatch → throw "Edit war! Copy your changes elsewhere for safekeeping and reload the page" and mutate nothing, not even tmod.

What each person sees. The winner: their text stands, their editor re-bases onto the new token (the success handler), so they can keep editing and saving normally. The loser: the sticky banner in the server's words; the recovery refresh repaints the view pane with the winner's text; their own words come back into the reopened editor, red, intact for copying. Their base is still stale on purpose — mashing SAVE just bounces loudly again; nobody's save ever silently overwrites an edit war they didn't see. The resolution is the banner's own instruction: copy your words, reload (a fresh load always shows the database — blurb drafts deliberately don't survive the tab), re-apply by hand.

Same-client rapid saves are a non-collision: they serialize on the client's op chain and each success re-bases before the next flies, so save-B-then-C from one browser lands in order.

All of it is pinned: the two-window clobber dance and repeat-SAVE bounce, the cletus/winifred story (foreign save mid-draft warns nobody; the collision surfaces at *his* save; reload shows only her words), stale-refusal-never-repaints-newer-draft, and the Firefox-ghost qual (stale cache + stale draft + moved blurb → clean load, no banner).

(First: the copy-split verification that was blocked last turn cleared — full suite green, 191 / 510 / 9 / 193.)

Problems with the spec, most serious first:

  1. Points 10–11 reintroduce the race that point 12 worries about. "Check the hash, then update" as two separate requests is check-then-act: two savers can both pass the check and both write, and the second silently clobbers the first — the exact lost-update the current design closed. The fix is what the code already does: the save *carries* the base token and the server compares-and-swaps atomically inside its script lock, one request, no window. The spec should read "SAVE sends the hash it started from; the server refuses atomically if it's stale." Point 12's answer is then: there are no race conditions left to have.
  1. Point 3's localStorage is the wrong scope for the base. The base must live exactly as long as the edit session (it's in dataset.base today). Persisting it invites the resurrection class of bug just exorcised — a stale base surviving a reload is the Firefox ghost with extra steps. In-memory, minted when the editor opens: yes; localStorage: no.
  1. Content hash vs. version token (points 3–4). A hash adds canonicalization headaches (client and server must hash identical bytes) and buys nothing over the existing opaque tblurb token, which already changes on every write. Point 4's optimization optimizes the wrong thing: Apps Script latency is ~all round-trip, not payload, and the client already receives full state every 5 s poll — a hash-only endpoint saves no time.
  1. Point 8 loses the words on a refused SAVE. "Pressing either makes the textarea disappear" is right for DISCARD and for a *successful* SAVE, but on an edit-war refusal the draft's only home would be the popup. Current behavior — editor stays open, red, words intact for copying — should survive into the spec.
  1. Point 7's DISCARD is the cancel button killed on 07-28 ("i hate these cancel buttons"). For the blurb alone it was originally floated, so maybe intended — but the reversal should be deliberate, not incidental.
  1. Point 13's diff popup is good — and undersold. With a rendered diff on screen, "stash and reload" is a weak resolution; this is exactly where MediaWiki offers the real choices (keep theirs / submit mine anyway, now informed). An explicit user choice in a diff view isn't the silent informed-overwrite that was rejected earlier. Also two copy notes: the popup title differs from the current banner copy whose single home is Code.gs's thrown string — one of them should own the words; and a VS-Code-style diff means vendoring or writing a small line-diff (Myers), which is fine but nonzero.
  1. Small ones. Point 3's refresh-on-pencil is good but shouldn't block the editor opening (open instantly; the ≤5s-stale poll plus CAS already backstops). Point 6's live preview repurposes the view pane from "server truth you'd be overwriting" to "your preview" — fine, since the diff popup takes over that job, but it's a real trade being made. Point 2's "standard markdown": the current renderer is a deliberate whitelist subset (no images/raw HTML — XSS surface in a shared field); worth stating in the spec if that's the intent.

Net: the architecture underneath the spec (atomic CAS with a server-minted token) should stay exactly as built; the spec's genuinely new material is the UI — pencil-refresh, side-by-side live preview, DISCARD, and the diff popup — and those are all buildable on the current mechanism unchanged.

Plain-language versions of the three ideas, then the README rewritten to match:

  1. How the client knows a refusal is an edit war. When a SAVE bounces, something must decide "show the edit-war popup" vs "show some other error." The fragile way is checking whether the error text contains "Edit war" — then rewording the message someday silently breaks the popup. The robust way needs no inspection at all: a blurb save can only be refused for two reasons (too long, or stale token), and the client already checks the length itself before sending. So any refusal that makes it back from the server *is* a collision, and the client can treat it as one unconditionally.
  1. Why the server's error text stops mattering. The server still throws an error sentence on a stale save, but the app never displays those words anymore — the popup brings its own title from stringles.js. The server's sentence is only ever seen by someone poking the API by hand with curl. So the old rule that server wording and client wording match verbatim is dead; each side words itself.
  1. The beat before the diff. Drawing the red/green diff requires the server's current blurb, which the client fetches when the refusal arrives — about a second. During that beat the popup's diff area is empty, so it shows the small hammering gavel (the app's waiting-for-data sign), with the usual 0.3-second delay so a fast fetch never flashes it. If that fetch itself fails, don't leave the gavel hammering forever: put the plain error text where the diff would have gone. The draft sits safe in the red textarea the whole time either way.

bug: on my phone i see "Awaiting bid..." after submitting my own bid. honestly there are so many little jankinesses like this it feels overwhelming. do you have any systematic way to clean things like this up?
14:33 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 2m10s

Root-caused. bidTip — and everything else about that cell — derives purely from state.bidders, which is *server* truth ([app.js:1499](app.js#L1499)). Between SUBMIT and the write settling (~3s against live Apps Script), the record has no bid, so your own row keeps saying "Awaiting bid...", the slot keeps its dashed breathing, the × stays offered, the padlock still says it's waiting on you. On a phone the tap-parked tooltip makes the lie prominent, and it stings precisely because dev is localhost where that window is ~0ms — this whole class of jank is invisible at development latency and glaring at production latency. Same root as the fresh-URL dead-screen bug.

The class, named: optimism asymmetry. Gestures paint instantly for everything backed by the local seats copy (adds, removes, renames) and for raw editor contents — but there is no local copy of *bidders*, so every surface derived from it (bid tip, slot→card flip, × graying, padlock state and tip, tab-title glyph) lags a full round trip while the commit pulse has already said "yours is away." Two truths on one row.

The systematic cleanup, three parts:

  1. One optimism convention, structurally. Give bids the same treatment seats already get: at SUBMIT the local picture gains the bid (bcount bumped, stamp now). Then the tip, the card flip, the ×, the padlock, and the title glyph all agree *by construction* — no per-surface patching, no "if in-flight" branches anywhere. Refusals already recover loudly (banner + words handed back + truth-repaint at settle). Race safety holds: reveal rides the same op chain, so it can't overtake your own flying bid, and the server refuses premature reveals regardless.
  1. Detect the class, not instances. The story bridge now has readDelay/opDelay levers — run the core journey at live-shaped latency (~1.5s per hop) and, after each commit gesture, sweep every visible text and tooltip for claims that contradict the gesture ("Awaiting" anything for an actor who just acted). That's a reusable jank audit like auditLayout/auditNames, and it would have caught both this bug and the fresh-URL one before you did.
  1. The matrix is small. State-derived surfaces: bid tip, bid cell look, ×, seal + tip, title glyph, legend, chronicle. Beats: draft → in-flight → settled → refused → revealed. That's ~a dozen assertions, not an ocean — the overwhelm is because instances surface one at a time on your phone, not because the class is large.

One decision before implementing, since it changes what the ledger claims: should your row show your bid as in the moment you press SUBMIT (recommended — it matches the seats convention and the pulse's own message), or should mid-flight get some distinct third look? The third look means styling and reasoning about a new state everywhere — anti-magic argues hard for the first.

how does anti-magic argue for showing a bid as "in" when it's not in?
14:37 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 49s

It doesn't — that was sloppy. Anti-magic only argues against the *third look* (a new visible state means new CSS, new tip copy, new quals, new reasoning on every surface). It says nothing about which of the two remaining renderings to pick, and "minimize code paths" never licenses asserting something false. Re-deriving honestly:

The real arguments for optimistic "in" are these, and none of them is anti-magic:

  1. The app already made this call for every other write. An add shows the row before the server confirms; a rename's comment in the code says it outright: committed is committed the moment you commit it, not when the server settles. Bids are currently the *one* write rendered record-faithfully — that asymmetry is the bug you hit. Whichever convention wins, one convention should.
  1. Your own signless-writes ruling. Writes fly with no busy sign because the commit pulse says "yours is away" and failures banner loudly. A ledger that says "Awaiting bid..." for three seconds after the pulse fired contradicts the pulse — the two signals you ruled sufficient are disagreeing with each other.
  1. Which falsehood misleads less. "Awaiting bid..." after SUBMIT is technically true of the record and functionally false to the reader — it reads as "your submit didn't take" a hundred percent of the time, and invites a confused re-submit. Optimistic "in" is a prediction that's wrong only when the write fails, and that failure already announces itself with a banner and your words handed back red. A 3-second prediction corrected loudly beats a 3-second literal truth that reads as a failure signal.

The counterargument, stated fairly: bids are the sacred object of this app, and there's a case that the *record* — who has actually bid, which gates the reveal — should never display ahead of itself. If that fidelity matters to you for bids specifically, then the honest cost is the third look (something like the commit pulse holding until settle instead of fading on its timer), and anti-magic just tells you to pay it in one place rather than per-surface.

Recommendation stands — optimistic "in" — but on grounds of the seats precedent, the signless ruling, and misleading-less, not anti-magic. The call is a design ruling, and it's yours.

would it be best-of-all-worlds to make this 3rd state subtly different, visually, to indicate that it's not server-confirmed yet?
14:43 Claude Code claude-fable-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m

Yes — and there's a version of it that costs almost nothing, because the third state already exists in disguise.

The commit pulse is currently a green tint keyed to a 0.6-second *timer* — an arbitrary beat that happens to feel right on localhost where settles are instant. Re-key that same tint to the *settle event*: it appears at SUBMIT (as now) and releases when the write lands (instead of when a timer says so). On dev latency that's visually identical to today. On live latency the tint holds the honest ~1–3 seconds, and its meaning sharpens from "you pressed a button just now" to "yours is away" — clearing is the confirmation. So the state count doesn't grow at all: {pulsing-for-0.6s, rest} becomes {away-until-settled, rest}. The lifetime of the existing transient becomes truthful instead of arbitrary. That's the anti-magic way to buy the third look.

This is also the convention users already know from messaging apps — optimistic bubble plus a subtle pending marker (WhatsApp's clock-then-ticks, iMessage's lighter bubble) that resolves quietly on delivery. Nobody reads it as a spinner, which keeps it inside the signless-writes ruling: no gray, no gavel, no blocked anything — the same pulse, honestly timed.

One boundary to be clear about: the subtlety only works for the *visual* cell. The other derived surfaces are binary and can't be subtly anything — the tooltip either says submitted or awaiting, the padlock either counts your bid or doesn't, the tab glyph either shows you as the blocker or not. Those go optimistic (count the flying bid), per the seats precedent; the tint on the card is what carries "not confirmed yet." Refusal recovery is unchanged and already loud: banner, words handed back red, tint cleared by the settle either way.

Recommendation: apply the settle-keyed pulse to all writes, not just bids — renames, adds, and blurb saves have the same in-flight window on live latency, and one convention beats two (the pulse node just needs to ride along to its op's settle). Red quals first, at live-shaped latency via the story bridge's delay levers: mid-flight, the row must read as bid-in everywhere (tip, ×, padlock) while the card wears the away-tint; at settle the tint clears; on a transport death the tint clears with the banner and the words come back.

Say go and it gets built.

Recommendation, firmed: optimistic bid view via overlay at the four sites, settle-keyed tint everywhere the pulse exists today, quals first at live-shaped latency. Ready on your go.

What it was. Not a loop — one long .stale stretch. The busy gavel's animation cycle holds a beat at each strike, so a pinned gavel reads as "spins, stops, spins more." The pin: a write queued while the arrival gray was still up (you type the add before the first server answer lands — easy at live Apps Script latency) made *every* incoming snapshot get discarded by the never-clobber guards in [app.js:434](app.js#L434-L455), and only the write's own settle could unpin. With Firefox's simultaneous add holding the server's script lock, Chrome's add settle stretched to many seconds — reproduced in real Chrome with live-shaped latency: gavel from keystroke to settle, exactly your description. Both browsers converge to the same roster afterward; the data was never in danger, only the busy sign lied about duration.

The fix ([app.js:446](app.js#L446-L455)): when the server answers for the current page but adoption must wait out an in-flight write, the gray retires immediately — the wire is alive and the optimistic picture is exactly as trustworthy as a calm page's, where the same add rides signless. In the re-run repro the gavel now retires at the arrival answer (~2s) instead of the contended settle (6s locally, plausibly 10–25s live). Per anti-magic, the fix's full conditional inventory: one new else if in refresh, plus one boolean (revealInFlight) guarding the single disclosed exception — the reveal's drumroll gray still belongs to the verdict and only its settle lifts it.

blurbver — and the architecture answer

Yes, it simplifies, and yes, a counter works strictly better than the timestamp. The old token was toISOString() + '/' + random tail — the code itself admitted "the token is for CAS identity, not chronology," with the random tail bolted on to dodge same-millisecond collisions. A counter incremented under the script lock cannot collide by construction, never consults a clock (this codebase already distrusts wall clocks — see the writeSeq comment), and the number is user-meaningful where the stamp never was: it IS the pencil's tooltip. The frozen-clock gas qual now proves CAS identity with Date.now() pinned — something the timestamp scheme could only pass via its random tail.

Shipped: auctions column 6 tblurb → blurbver (0 = never described, born explicitly, '' cells refuse as corruption), the CAS compares integers, refusals still carry the full snapshot for the war diff, and the pencil wears "Auction description, version N" — which supersedes the recorded 07-17 no-pencil-tip ruling, so that qual flipped accordingly. One anti-postel tightening to flag: '' is no longer accepted as a spelling of the virgin base (it would coerce to 0 silently); the only virgin is the number 0.

Deploy note: this is a schema change — npm run deploy will fail its live smoke with delete-the-auctions-tab marching orders until the tab is deleted (the drift armor working as designed). Code.gs is edited but not deployed.
